meta.title: Overview
meta.description: What React Scheduler is, what it renders, how it is controlled, and where to go next. MIT licensed, with no paid tier.

introduction.what: React Scheduler shows a working day as a schedule. It takes a flat list of items with a start, a level and a title, groups them into the shifts of the day, and renders them either as a list you read from top to bottom or as a timeline where an item's height is its duration. It is one React component, written in TypeScript, HTML and CSS, with no runtime dependencies beyond React itself.
introduction.controlled: Everything is controlled from the outside. Props set the data, the shifts and the options; CSS variables set the colors, the spacing and the density; callbacks report every change; <link to="/customization/slots/">slots</link> and render props replace any part of the markup. The whole state can be left to the component or held by your application, prop by prop.
introduction.not: It is not a calendar and not an editor. There is no month or year grid, no drag-and-drop, no recurrence, no time zone of its own and no data layer: it renders the items you give it, for the day you ask for, and tells you when the reader does something.

points: Accessible by construction: every card is a button, every shift a heading, every dialog focus-trapped, and the target is WCAG 2.2 AA — checked by axe in the package’s browser tests and on the pages of this site.

Themed without a UI kit: two presets, three densities, a light and a dark scheme, and more than a hundred and fifty CSS variables. No CSS-in-JS runtime, no utility-class library, nothing to configure before the first render.
Zero runtime dependencies: only react and react-dom as peers. Nothing else is installed with it, so nothing else can break it.
Safe on the server: it renders on the server without touching the DOM, hydrates without a warning, and starts its observers only once mounted.
Small and lazy: around 25 kB gzipped for the main entry, with the overflow dialog and the detail dialog split into chunks that load when they are first opened.
Seven languages built in: English, Romanian, Hungarian, Spanish, French, German and Portuguese, each a plain object you can extend or replace.
